**Before the appointment**
- Add the appointment date in the Appointment tab. MenoMap shows how ready your notes are and what would make them more complete.
- Choose the most important topics and questions. Limit yourself to three or four.
- Create your notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**At the appointment**
- Hand over or show the first page. It was designed to be read in under a minute: counts, averages, the heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If the health professional who looks after you speaks another language, you can create the notes in that language.

**What the notes are, and what they are not**

They are a summary of what you logged, plus what you chose to bring from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis or a complete clinical record, and the patterns they include are coincidence checks, not proof of cause. The health professional may ask questions the notes cannot answer, and that is normal.

**After the appointment**

Add any new medication with its start date. Within a few weeks, MenoMap can show your logs from before and after, which makes the next review easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single moment in time: the day that marks 12 months in a row without a period, when that is not explained by something else (such as pregnancy, some medications or surgery). In many countries it happens, on average, in the early 50s, but it is common at any time between the mid-40s and mid-50s.

**Perimenopause** is the period of years leading up to that moment. Hormone levels rise and fall irregularly, so periods may become irregular, heavier, lighter, closer together or further apart. Many of the changes associated with menopause, such as hot flushes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, often start here, while there are still periods. Perimenopause can last a few years or considerably longer, and it is different from person to person.

**Post-menopause** is everything that comes after those 12 months. Some symptoms calm down over time; others may continue for years.

Menopause can also happen earlier due to surgery that removes the ovaries, some cancer treatments or other health problems. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth talking about with a health professional.

**How it is recognised.** In many people over 45, health professionals recognise perimenopause or menopause from the clinical history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always necessary, because hormone levels vary from day to day. They are more likely to be used when the person is younger or the picture is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you what stage you are at. What it can do is keep an honest record of what you notice: waves, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and the health professional can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Health professionals call hot flushes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flush is a sudden wave of heat, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with flushing, sweating, a racing heart or a chill afterwards. Night sweats are the same thing during sleep, and can be strong enough to wake you or soak the sheets.

They are among the most common changes around menopause. Some people have few and mild ones; others have many a day, disrupting work and sleep. In some people they disappear after a few years; in others they last much longer.

**What can make them more likely.** Many people notice patterns with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress or heavy bedding. This varies a lot from person to person, which is why logging your own tags can be more useful than a general list.

**There are other causes.** Flushing and sweating can also result from thyroid problems, infections, some medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not follow the usual pattern, or come with weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, talk about it with a health professional.

**Describing them well.** Useful details for an appointment:
- How many you have per day and per night, roughly
- How intense they are and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What seems to happen before them
- What you have already tried, and whether anything changed

MenoMap's Wave button and the later log exist precisely to capture this without much effort.

**Help is available.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, as well as practical approaches. Which are most suitable for you is a conversation to have with a health professional.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) replaces some of the oestrogen that the body produces less of around menopause. The main clinical guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flushes and night sweats in many people, and it may help with other symptoms too.

**It comes in different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets and low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms such as dryness. Someone who still has a womb is usually prescribed a progestogen along with the oestrogen, to protect the lining of the womb.

**The benefits and risks depend on the person:** age, time since periods stopped, personal and family history (for example of breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease), and the type and route of the treatment. That is why it is a decision to make with a health professional who knows your history, and not something an app can decide.

**Questions people often ask:**
- Is hormone therapy an option for me, and why or why not?
- What type and form do you suggest, and why?
- What benefits can I expect, and after how long?
- What are my personal risks, and how do they compare with not having treatment?
- What signs should I watch for, and when should we review the treatment?

**If you already take this treatment,** log it in MenoMap (Profile → Medication). MenoMap will show your waves before and after you started, as a coincidence check and not as proof, so you have something concrete to discuss at the review.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not suitable for everyone, and some people simply prefer other paths. There are several.

**Prescription options.** Some non-hormonal medications have evidence that they reduce hot flushes. They include certain medications originally developed for other conditions and a newer class created specifically for hot flushes. Each has its benefits, side effects and interactions, so a health professional can help you weigh them.

**Talking therapies and mind-body approaches.** Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adapted to menopause has evidence that it makes hot flushes and night sweats less bothersome and that it improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes that people find helpful:**
- Layers of clothing you can take off quickly
- A fan on the desk and beside the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Noticing your triggers and reducing them (MenoMap's tags and experiments help here)
- Regular physical activity and a steady sleep routine

**Supplements and plant-based products.** The evidence is inconsistent or limited for many of them, quality varies and some interact with other medications. Tell the health professional or the pharmacist everything you take, including over-the-counter products.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own records before and during a change, which is easier to judge than a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short, and it is hard to remember a month of nights on the spot. People tend to remember the most recent days or the worst ones. A simple log fills that gap.

**What a diary gives the health professional:**
- How often symptoms happen and how intense they are, and not just that they happen
- Whether things are getting better, getting worse or staying the same
- What was going on around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A starting point for comparison, if you try a treatment

**Keep it light.** A diary only helps if you keep it up. MenoMap was built around a one-tap Wave button and a four-question night check-in, so it takes seconds, not a whole notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of records usually show a clearer picture than a single bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. MenoMap's Appointment tab helps you choose questions and prints them with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
After you have gone 12 months without a period, **any vaginal bleeding should be evaluated by a health professional**, even if it happened only once, and even if it was just a small loss or a pink or brownish discharge.

Most of the time, the cause turns out not to be serious. Thinning of the lining of the vagina or womb, for example, is common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat when detected early. That is why public health guidance says to have it evaluated rather than wait.

**If you are on hormone therapy,** some bleeding patterns may be expected, depending on the type you are on. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, heavier than usual or outside the expected time should also be evaluated.

**What to do:**
- Contact your health professional or health service and say that you have had bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, the amount and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can save this for you (Profile → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding happened. It will remind you to have it evaluated and include it in your appointment notes.

backTranslations.529:
Sleeping badly is one of the most common complaints in midlife, and it rarely has a single cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly, or leave you too hot or damp to fall asleep again.

**Other common factors:**
- Needing to urinate during the night
- Anxiety or a racing mind
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but tends to fragment the second half of the night
- Caffeine late in the day
- Pain, restless legs or the snoring of whoever sleeps with you
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which can be a sign of sleep apnoea (worth talking about, especially if you are very sleepy during the day)

**What usually helps.** A cool, dark bedroom; breathable bedding and layers you can take off; a steady wake-up time; and less alcohol near bedtime. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied approach, and many health professionals can refer you to it.

**What to log.** For a week or two, note your sleep score, night waves, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's night check-in and wave log do this in a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside your night sweats, as context and not as an explanation.

**When to seek assessment.** Talk to a health professional if sleeping badly is affecting your safety (for example, while driving), your mood or your daily life, or if you notice pauses in breathing or that you wake up gasping during the night.
